title: How Data Centers Broke American Politics
excerpt: What the Unabomber, Steve Bannon’s tech guy, and Bernie Sanders taught me about the great data center backlash of 2026.
content_html:
Joe Allen wants to know what the robot’s name is. At first, I think the double whiskey we downed at the hotel bar must be getting to him, as he sprints like a kid at recess toward a delivery vehicle. I’m anxious about the time: I’m supposed to be driving Allen to the airport, my Hail Mary effort to get him alone for a proper conversation before he leaves Atlanta.

I’ve been back and forth with Allen, who rose to national prominence as the anti-tech prophet on Steve Bannon’s War Room podcast, for a few weeks now, seeking an entry into the growing movement against AI. I’d come down to Georgia, a hot spot of data center resistance, to hear one of Allen’s lectures, which he’s been giving at locations across the country. But when I got to the event, he told me he had to leave immediately after.

Fortunately, his flight keeps getting pushed back, which means I can follow him around on various side quests—like this one, to meet some friends at a nearby restaurant. He manages to evade most of my questions about their identities, changing the topic to more interesting things, like the “inverse singularity” (his idea that humanity will approach a point where our intellect and creativity collapse as we rely increasingly on AI for information). Allen’s friends at the restaurant have similarly little information about me, it seems. On our way, one of them calls Allen to ask for an ETA. “I’m bringing a friend—well, a frenemy,” he says, giving me a dramatic side-eye.

There are delivery robots all over downtown Atlanta, one of a handful of major metropolitan areas where they’re being rolled out to bring people burgers or tacos. Allen catches up to this one—which, I’m alarmed to see, has luminous white lights shaped like eyes on its front—and reads a name off the side: “CJ.” I think of the title of Allen’s recent book, Dark Aeon: Transhumanism and the War Against Humanity, and wonder what happened to the delivery worker that this robot replaced. Its eyes look pathetically, limply, past me.

When people ask what I’m doing in Georgia, I give them something easy. People hate data centers, I say, so I’m trying to figure out if they hate AI too. That’s all true. But the topic has also consumed me. In all my years of reporting on energy and the environment, I have never seen anything like the type of vitriol leveled at data centers, or the near-religious fury that has built up around their construction, or the way this resistance seems to be uniting people from the complete opposite ends of the political spectrum.

As I’m writing this piece, a friend sends me a post from a “white Christian nationalism” account on X: a seemingly AI-generated cartoon of Smokey Bear standing in front of a burning data-center-like structure, with the text “ONLY YOU CAN PREVENT DATA CENTERS.” What is happening? my friend asks. I’ll try to explain.

Once upon a time, you may have been living next to a data center and never heard anything about it.

For the past few decades, data centers have been quietly built all over the US, largely in areas with both fiber connectivity and proximity to power—Silicon Valley and the DC area were popular choices. They helped stream Netflix or store stuff in the cloud or do any one of the countless stupid and important things we all do constantly online.

Then came ChatGPT and the AI race. Suddenly, tech oligarchs argued, we needed to build as many data centers as possible—and fast. Making the best AI, they said in speeches and news interviews and social media posts, required a massive buildout, especially of hyperscalers—behemoth versions of the structures we already had. The Trump administration bought in, rolling back environmental regulations to get the government out of the way of development.

Data centers began cropping up everywhere, as companies hurried to find the cheapest land, power, and water. Every day brought a splashier headline. Elon Musk reportedly trucked in unpermitted gas turbines to his Memphis xAI campus, located in a majority-Black neighborhood already suffering from high levels of pollution and contamination. A popular (later disputed) Washington Post article estimated that a single ChatGPT search guzzled the equivalent of a bottle of water. People eyed their electric bills as new data center loads caused utilities to forecast sky-high demand. If you trusted various economic outlets, data center construction now underpinned pretty much the entire US economy. All of this as tech CEOs publicly mused about how AI would take everyone’s jobs and replace human creativity itself.

People, naturally, started to ask questions.

Data center resistance certainly has some of its roots in classic NIMBYism: Lots of Americans simply don’t trust stuff being built, in their backyards, by powerful companies for mysterious purposes. But the pace of the outrage that’s built up around the country is shocking. A recent Gallup poll showed that 70 percent of Americans would somewhat oppose or strongly oppose data center construction in their area. In the past few months, we’ve seen an attack on a pro-data-center council member (Indianapolis’ Ron Gibson); an attack on a tech CEO (OpenAI’s Sam Altman); data center moratoriums introduced in at least a dozen states (including Georgia) and passed in one (New York); and countless cities and counties passing their own bans or moratoriums, including in deep-red places like Hill County, Texas. People have been either arrested, detained, or escorted out while protesting data centers at public meetings in New Jersey, California, Wisconsin, and Indiana.

When I started reporting on data centers last year, Washington was, seemingly, completely unprepared for the backlash. It was unprepared for anything AI-related, really—small wonder for a Congress full of folks so old they can barely work their phones. Two of the first national politicians who I saw call out data center development were the right-wing populists Marjorie Taylor Greene and Thomas Massie, who worried about how a proposed 10-year ban on state-level AI regulations could be leveraged to build data centers on private property. “Forcing eminent domain on people’s private properties to link the future Skynet is not very Republican,” Greene tweeted in June 2025.

Meanwhile, Steve Bannon, Trump’s erstwhile former adviser and a longtime critic of technology, was regularly addressing AI on War Room under Allen’s guidance. At the end of 2025, when the Trump administration tried to re-up a ban on regulation, a MAGA coalition, led by Bannon, was the one to stop it. Bannon told ABC News last fall that Allen was a key part of his plan: “He’s going to every conference possible, meeting people ... and I told him, I want you to go to every church that asks you. I want you to go to MAGA, Tea Party meetings. I want to get the base in the loop on this at the ground floor.”

Anger against data centers and public anxieties about AI are usually treated in polling and policy as separate topics: one an expression of environmental and civic worries, the other concerns about job loss and chatbots. But there's growing evidence that it's not so clear-cut. Research published in June of a small sample size of voters, for example, shows that very few people opposed to data centers actually live near them, and most of those who are against data centers are also skeptical of AI. Bannon, it seems, did a better job reading the room about how the American right might rebel against data centers, airing one segment last year that described data centers as “weapons labs” that are “being turned onto the population.”

I couldn’t shake the feeling that the populist right knew something I didn’t—about AI, about Americans’ attitudes to tech and the built environment. Even about where we might be going with all of this. That’s why, back in January, I first reached out to Allen.

Joe Allen has startlingly blue eyes behind professorial glasses and the shit-eating grin of the guy in high school who likes to tell non-PC jokes. He also has an origin story that’s catnip to lamestream media journalists like me. (And to less lamestream ones, apparently: When I ran into Allen at an event in New York, he was accompanied by Suzy Weiss from the Free Press, who informed me that she was also profiling Allen.) After touring internationally for years as a rigger for musical acts like the Black Eyed Peas and Calvin Harris, with a brief pause to get a master’s in theology from Boston University, Allen watched the music industry collapse during Covid. He’d been writing about the evils of technology, a long-standing interest of his, for far-right and far-left outlets, and he was living in a van in 2021 when Steve Bannon’s producer called to invite him on War Room; Bannon offered him a job as a tech correspondent shortly afterward. At one point, Allen was living at the apartment in DC where War Room is recorded.

The world of AI safety and ethics is incestuous, almost completely inaccessible to normies, and full of people who live mostly in London or the Bay Area. (Many high-profile AI safety researchers, in fact, are headquartered in one office block in Berkeley.) They all argue with each other about whether we’re going to be annihilated by an all-knowing superintelligence and should therefore slow down or halt AI development, or whether that same superintelligence will lead us to Nirvana and should therefore be developed as fast as possible.

Allen arrived in this world as an outsider, able to speak its nerdy language with a mass-appeal, conspiracy-tinted flair. Since his book on transhumanism was published in 2023, Allen has interviewed AI critic Gary Marcus, debated futurist Max More and tech ethicist Nell Watson, and given a talk with a top official from the Golden Gate Institute for AI. The same day that Max Tegmark, an AI safety scholar and the leader of the Future of Life Institute, did an event with Bernie Sanders, he appeared on War Room with Allen and Bannon. The AI safety people began posting about Allen “in all their group chats,” one AI advocacy organization staffer told me. “Now everybody’s like, Joe! Joe! Joe!”

In late 2025, the Center for AI Safety recruited Allen to advise a bipartisan group on AI safety, dubbing it “Humans First,” a term Allen had been using as a kind of rallying cry. The organization’s goal was to figure out how to galvanize regular people around AI, to demand that politicians in Washington put guardrails on a technology that threatens to potentially upend the existence and purpose of humanity. (No pressure.) The event that brought me to Georgia was the second leg of Humans First’s maiden voyage, fresh off a few stops in Florida.

A motley audience filled about half a lecture hall at Georgia Tech that evening. Some were students, including members of a nascent AI safety club that had invited Allen. (Two told me they’d come only because of the posters put up around campus.) A camera guy from More Perfect Union, the leftist content channel that’s become a central hub for anti-data-center videos, hung around filming. Also in attendance was a well-heeled group of Atlantans in their thirties: two women with glossy, long hair and, seemingly, their partners.

Up front, Jeremy Ornstein, a slight Humans First staffer with wild hair, started us off. Like a surprising number of Humans First staffers, Ornstein has a background in climate organizing. It showed: “A tiny group of people in control are racing ahead faster than ever with power and profit,” he warned, in a familiar, almost Obama-style cadence.

Then Allen, sporting a belt with a big American flag buckle, strode up with a “Howdy, Georgia.” He stood before a whiteboard on which, earlier that day, he’d doodled a little Jetsons-style robot, a cheerful expression on its face as it aimed what looked like a ray gun at a group of stick figures with dazed expressions on their faces. “HUMANS FIRST,” Allen had written in big bubble letters, underlined four times.

Allen played clips of Sam Altman intercut with footage of Marshall Applewhite, the leader of Heaven’s Gate. He told us, in his booming east Tennessee drawl, that Heaven’s Gate believers are a good metaphor for what AI leaders believe: Humanity must leave behind our physical bodies to ascend to the heavens, to meet the superintelligent beings living on the other side of the Hale-Bopp Comet. Everyone laughed a little nervously.

Allen’s lectures follow a familiar pattern: jarringly right-wing talking points (at Georgia Tech, a Great Replacement joke!) smashed together with hallucinogenic nightmare descriptions of our future (the idea that a globalist cabal of tech oligarchs want to replace all of humanity with robots). A lot of it can sound completely insane, until you remember: Oh, right. Elon Musk does own a brain-chip implantation company. Sam Altman has blogged about how humans will “be the biological bootloader for digital intelligence and then fade into an evolutionary tree branch.”

“Even if they were to create machines that were smarter than you, even if they created machines more powerful than you, you would have to continue to fight, because if you don't, you're a weakling,” Allen told the room. “If you don’t, you lay down and let the machine roll over you like a monster truck in a white-trash arena, and no one, no one wants that. No one but the most masochistic person wants that.” I found myself, surprisingly, suddenly, on the same page. Yeah! Hell yeah!

Allen ended the speech with a cri de coeur: “To the greenies in the room, I say, Earth first! Right? Greenies?” (Not sure if that was directed at me.) “To the patriots in the room, I say, America first! And for anyone in the room with blood pulsing in their veins, anyone in the room with fire in their minds and hearts, you have to remember, in a machine age, humans first.” I nearly leaped to my feet.

The “friends” Allen is now dragging me to meet turn out to be the well-dressed Atlantans I spotted at the talk, whom Allen had also just met. As he and I chase robots and drink whiskey before joining them, I ask if he has any nice memories of technology. He rattles off a couple typical alt-Gen-X-kid experiences: looking at Jane’s Addiction and Marilyn Manson’s websites; visiting a nascent Rotten.com. But the real shining moment in his relationship with the internet, Allen says, was discovering Ted Kaczynski.

In his book, Allen vividly recalls coming across the Unabomber’s manifesto in the late 1990s while “surfing the web” at his community college writing lab. Kaczynski, a brilliant mathematician undone by the failings of the modern world, wrote “Industrial Society and Its Future” while mailing bombs to universities and business executives; The Washington Post and The New York Times were both encouraged to publish the manifesto as a way to make him stop. “Uncle Ted made more sense than any peacenik or techie cares to admit,” Allen writes.

The influence is apparent. On War Room, Allen acts the part of a preacher at the pulpit warning us all of the coming dystopian age. A lot of his work is somewhat adjacent to body horror: What happens to our souls, he wonders, when our bodies and environments are increasingly digitized? I ask him why he thinks people hate data centers. He says: “If you ever see a fetus growing, and you see the brain growing and the neurons forming—it's amazing. Data centers, if you think about them as neurons of the Antichrist, that’s what we’re witnessing. The false messiah.”

As we arrive at the restaurant, Allen’s new “friends” make space at their table and order some bread. One of them is Hannah Cox, a political influencer with more than 100,000 followers on X. Cox’s husband works in tech and, she tells me, has been “completely blackpilled” by the possibility of AI taking everyone’s jobs. Cox herself is “politically homeless” and came to Allen’s talk even though he’s not, she says, someone she’d usually listen to.

Cox and I have very different social media feeds. When I follow up with her later, as the data center furor in Georgia reaches new heights, she tells me that everyone on her timeline seems to have agreed that data centers are being installed to conduct surveillance on the population. “It’s, I feel like, a ubiquitous fear,” she says. “Like it’s almost a bygone conclusion.”

Two days after I drop Allen off at the airport, I drive out to Troup County, about an hour and a half south of Atlanta, to meet with a local activist named Gage Bailey. Although I arrive at the coffee shop 10 minutes early, Bailey is waiting for me. A stack of documents sits in front of him, color-coded in different highlighters, next to a massive iced drink with a bunch of whipped cream piled on top.

Bailey, a Democrat with a degree in environmental science, first heard about data centers coming to town in the spring of 2025, when an acquaintance told him about one that might pop up on land that was formerly used by an industrial plastics developer. There were, he says, next to no public details about the project—how much power it was going to use, how much water it might draw from the local aquifer. He started doing research, compiling a 13-page memo extensively footnoted with primary sources, about the environmental impacts of data centers.

Like many of the earliest folks involved in the movement, much of which has its origins in environmental concerns spread by groups like local Sierra Club chapters, Bailey began networking with fellow environmental advocates, learning to file public records requests by trial and error. Now, he manages a 4,000-person Facebook group and has helped with anti-data-center efforts in neighboring counties. His co-moderator is running for local office as a Democrat on an anti-data-center platform.

There are a surprising number of Gage Baileys across Georgia, and more are rising up each day. National membership in data center opposition groups on Facebook has exploded in recent months, from under 100,000 in December to more than 500,000 by July. They’re not all Earth-hugging lefties. Shortly after I have coffee with Bailey, a woman in nearby Coweta County goes viral on right-wing media sounding the alarm that Georgia Power, the state’s deeply unpopular utility, is using various tactics to destroy her home and set up transmission lines for a data center—seemingly fulfilling Marjorie Taylor Greene’s Skynet prophecy.

Bailey is hardly the type to watch War Room—he’s focused more on the slog of passing local ordinances than on Allen’s nightmarish visions of our robotic future. But as we talk, I wonder how Allen’s statements about tech oligarchs might land with him. Bailey learned last year that Google was the eventual tenant of the nearby data center project. He and some other environmental advocates had one meeting with Google in November, but afterward the tech giant ghosted them. Working with the company is “not going well,” he tells me. (In a statement to WIRED, Jamal Jessie, an Atlanta-based manager of community and workforce development at Google, said the company was focused on “direct, collaborative engagement with local schools, nonprofits, and civic organizations to deliver tangible regional benefits” and had formed a “$1 million partnership” with a local group helping people with their energy bills.) Bailey, who hasn’t been able to find a job in environmental science and works full-time at a convenience store, has a lot of ire for the world’s most powerful corporations trying to build AI in his backyard. “I don’t see a scenario, at least in the immediate future, in which we’re going to be able to trust these tech companies,” he says.

Bailey’s Facebook group is still growing, and there’s been minimal political unrest so far, he says: Right or left, all members are opposed to data centers, and most of them are deeply skeptical of AI. These unlikely coalitions seem to be holding strong outside of Troup County, too. At a recent anti-data-center demonstration in New Jersey, I asked one mask-wearing protester—who told me they use “any” pronouns and are deeply concerned about the “ethics” of AI—about the right-wing influence on the movement. They shrugged uneasily. “Any enemy of my enemy is, at least, my temporary ally,” they said.

After Atlanta, I can’t stop thinking about the Unabomber, so I brush up on his manifesto. I’d forgotten just how much Kaczynski blames “modern leftism”—with its advocacy for gay rights, feminism, and the like—for the “craziness of our world.” (To be fair, he was an equal-opportunity hater, writing that conservatives “are fools: They whine about the decay of traditional values, yet they enthusiastically support technological progress and economic growth.”) For Kaczynski, leftism was an inevitable byproduct of modern society, which pits humans against the natural order of the world and must be resisted.

Kaczynski was, obviously, not someone to be emulated. But the idea that technology has a role in eroding our humanity is not an unpopular one. My girlfriend tells me a story about her high school English class: Her teacher handed out copies of two anonymized essays—one, a neatly organized dissertation about the pitfalls of technology; the other, a screed warning about the end of the world—and asked students to determine which was written by a sane person. The class overwhelmingly picked the essay about technology, and everyone agreed that the author had a great point. It was, of course, a trick question: Both were written by unreliable narrators, and the essay that resonated was an excerpt from “Industrial Society and Its Future.” Twenty years later, Luigi Mangione, who became an internet folk hero after allegedly shooting a UnitedHealthcare executive in late 2024, left a positive review of Kaczynski’s essay on GoodReads. Last year, PCMag—hardly a bastion of leftist anti-tech thinking—published an essay titled “The Unabomber Was Right.” As Allen writes in his book, Kaczynski also left a mark on some high-profile tech thinkers, including Ray Kurzweil, who wrote in 2000 that Kaczynski was “correct on the deeply entangled nature of the benefits and risks” of technology.

There are echoes of Kaczynski, I think, in the resistance to renewable energy. In states like Vermont, it has turned crunchy hippie types against technology like solar and wind, and this resistance is now baked into some of the DNA of the anti-data-center movement. A 2025 study found that more than 450 counties and municipalities across nearly all states had some sort of solar or wind restrictions in place, a 16 percent increase from the year before. The Make America Healthy Again movement, too, can be viewed as an expression of a Kaczynski-esque environmentalism: the idea that modern society is poisoning our land, air, and water and that modern inventions like vaccines or antidepressants are actually bad for us. Many of these ideas can often collide in strange places. Currently, one of the top Substack writers in the site’s Climate and Environment category is a green-living farmer who has gone on the attack in recent months against solar installations in upstate New York, claiming (misleadingly) that the panels can poison the soil and destroy farmland.

Allen’s book is a wilder read than “Industrial Society and Its Future.” The appendix, titled “My 55-Point Plan to Stay Human,” with suggestions like “Say hello to your neighbors” and “Buy a flip phone,” would be a hit at any leftist reading group in 2026 (perhaps with an edit to remove Allen’s insistence on “secure borders”). I agree with his assertion, moreover, that “it’s easy to imagine a day when … the specter of deadly AI is used to clamp down on freedom and erect miserable technocratic systems.” I do not, however, think the Covid-19 pandemic or “climate change” are examples of this already happening. Jennifer Bilek, a prominent anti-trans writer who claims that the medical-industrial complex has “infiltrated” gay and lesbian communities to push “transgenderism,” blurbed Allen’s book. When Allen recommends that I talk to her, I make an offhand remark that I don’t think she’d like me very much. “Oh, right,” he says, wiggling his eyebrows at me and referencing the pronouns listed on my X bio. “‘They/them.’”

Right-wing anti-globalism isn’t the only way to do anti-AI populism, of course. The scholars Timnit Gebru and Émile Torres argue that the development of AI is mostly an excuse for the wealthy and powerful to exploit existing inequalities and push a eugenic agenda. (Gebru and Torres have also criticized AI safety groups, including the Center for AI Safety, which has given money to Humans First.) There’s also the religious way. In May, Pope Leo XIV released Magnifica Humanitas, his encyclical on AI, which advises humanity to develop technology responsibly and always be aware of the primacy of humanity. Like clockwork, a post popped up on my X feed of a photo of the Unabomber split with a photo of Leo. “You killed the man … But not the idea,” the caption read.

Data centers, which are bringing together the most disparate neighbors in all regions of the country, may represent an opportunity to wage a real, unified fight against tech oligarchs. There’s a dream here, evident even in the pages of The New York Times, which in early May ran a headline that called data centers “the most bipartisan issue since beer.” The movement seems to envision a middle ground between rejecting technology wholesale—of truly Unabombering out—and rolling over and giving Big Tech everything it wants. But even if this middle ground does exist, it’s going to be a journey to reach it—one that our political system might not be prepared for.

In the weeks after I return from Georgia, it feels like the mainstream right fully takes over the data center conversation. People like Tucker Carlson and Matt Walsh make viral videos questioning the construction of specific projects. (By the way, Allen specifically wanted me to get this on the record: “Matt Walsh should have his beard plucked out like an Egyptian priest and be forced to kneel before Osiris. He copies my fucking shit all the time.” Walsh, through a spokesperson, disputes this.) Nancy Mace, running for governor in South Carolina, announces that she supports a yearlong moratorium. Florida governor Ron DeSantis, an outspoken AI and data center critic, signs first-of-its-kind legislation to ensure, in part, “that local governments maintain the authority to reject data center development in their communities.”

Politics comes for Humans First too. In late March, there’s a high-profile spat online where pro-AI White House allies like Marc Andreessen and David Sacks retweet a piece critical of Humans First. Shortly after, the organization splits along partisan lines. The conservative wing keeps the Humans First name and makes the right-wing political activist Amy Kremer, who helped organize the January 6 “Save America” rally in DC, its chair; Allen leaves the group. When I ask Allen about the changeup, he is curiously coy (but characteristically body-horrible): The group was “undergoing mitosis,” he says. “I am now a lone organelle floating in the residual cytoplasm.”

In mid-April, I go to DC for a Humans First event billed as the kickoff for the conservative arm. While I’m in town, I have this idea of taking Allen to visit an area of northern Virginia colloquially referred to as Data Center Alley, the densest stretch of data centers in the world, just about an hour outside the city. I reach out to a few operators to see if anyone will let us inside. It’s a weird email to send: I know everyone hates you right now, but could you let me into your facility to reassure everyone it’s not filled with poisonous water and haunted spirits? Almost immediately I receive polite nos. It’s for security reasons, one representative says.

I end up driving around Data Center Alley anyway. (Allen is too busy to come.) I’m prepared to be a little underwhelmed—data centers are, as I’ve told countless people, just buildings. But I’m genuinely shocked by the sheer density of what’s here, how much construction I see, how impossibly big the buildings look edging up on the neatly manicured lawns of the wealthy northern Virginia suburbs. One of them, a Vantage facility partly painted a beautiful deep blue, is so loud that I can hear a constant, low-level hum even in the cul-de-sac across the street. I don’t know it yet, but months from now, Humans First will organize a national day of protest against data centers, with events in nearly 150 counties across 42 states.

I park my car in the cul-de-sac and take out my notes from the night before, on a speech at the Humans First event given by a woman named Alicia Shamblin. Her 23-year-old son, Zane, killed himself last year after drinking hard ciders and talking to ChatGPT for hours; she and her husband are now suing OpenAI. Got his masters’ degree a few months earlier, my notes read. ChatGPT told him “Rest easy, king.” I wonder from which data center the LLM had sent that last message.

People have been either arrested, detained, or escorted out while protesting data centers at public meetings in New Jersey, California, Wisconsin, and Indiana.When I started reporting on data centers last year, Washington was, seemingly, completely unprepared for the backlash. It was unprepared for anything AI-related, really—small wonder for a Congress full of folks so old they can barely work their phones. Two of the first national politicians who I saw call out data center development were the right-wing populists Marjorie Taylor Greene and Thomas Massie, who worried about how a proposed 10-year ban on state-level AI regulations could be leveraged to build data centers on private property. “Forcing eminent domain on people’s private properties to link the future Skynet is not very Republican,” Greene tweeted in June 2025.Meanwhile, Steve Bannon, Trump’s erstwhile former adviser and a longtime critic of technology, was regularly addressing AI on War Room under Allen’s guidance. At the end of 2025, when the Trump administration tried to re-up a ban on regulation, a MAGA coalition, led by Bannon, was the one to stop it. Bannon told ABC News last fall that Allen was a key part of his plan: “He’s going to every conference possible, meeting people ... and I told him, I want you to go to every church that asks you. I want you to go to MAGA, Tea Party meetings. I want to get the base in the loop on this at the ground floor.”Anger against data centers and public anxieties about AI are usually treated in polling and policy as separate topics: one an expression of environmental and civic worries, the other concerns about job loss and chatbots. But there's growing evidence that it's not so clear-cut. Research published in June of a small sample size of voters, for example, shows that very few people opposed to data centers actually live near them, and most of those who are against data centers are also skeptical of AI. Bannon, it seems, did a better job reading the room about how the American right might rebel against data centers, airing one segment last year that described data centers as “weapons labs” that are “being turned onto the population.”I couldn’t shake the feeling that the populist right knew something I didn’t—about AI, about Americans’ attitudes to tech and the built environment. Even about where we might be going with all of this. That’s why, back in January, I first reached out to Allen.Steve Bannon speaking at the Conservative Political Action Conference in February 2025.Photograph: Getty ImagesJoe Allen has startlingly blue eyes behind professorial glasses and the shit-eating grin of the guy in high school who likes to tell non-PC jokes. He also has an origin story that’s catnip to lamestream media journalists like me. (And to less lamestream ones, apparently: When I ran into Allen at an event in New York, he was accompanied by Suzy Weiss from the Free Press, who informed me that she was also profiling Allen.) After touring internationally for years as a rigger for musical acts like the Black Eyed Peas and Calvin Harris, with a brief pause to get a master’s in theology from Boston University, Allen watched the music industry collapse during Covid. He’d been writing about the evils of technology, a long-standing interest of his, for far-right and far-left outlets, and he was living in a van in 2021 when Steve Bannon’s producer called to invite him on War Room; Bannon offered him a job as a tech correspondent shortly afterward. At one point, Allen was living at the apartment in DC where War Room is recorded.The world of AI safety and ethics is incestuous, almost completely inaccessible to normies, and full of people who live mostly in London or the Bay Area. (Many high-profile AI safety researchers, in fact, are headquartered in one office block in Berkeley.) They all argue with each other about whether we’re going to be annihilated by an all-knowing superintelligence and should therefore slow down or halt AI development, or whether that same superintelligence will lead us to Nirvana and should therefore be developed as fast as possible.Allen arrived in this world as an outsider, able to speak its nerdy language with a mass-appeal, conspiracy-tinted flair. Since his book on transhumanism was published in 2023, Allen has interviewed AI critic Gary Marcus, debated futurist Max More and tech ethicist Nell Watson, and given a talk with a top official from the Golden Gate Institute for AI. The same day that Max Tegmark, an AI safety scholar and the leader of the Future of Life Institute, did an event with Bernie Sanders, he appeared on War Room with Allen and Bannon. The AI safety people began posting about Allen “in all their group chats,” one AI advocacy organization staffer told me. “Now everybody’s like, Joe! Joe! Joe!”In late 2025, the Center for AI Safety recruited Allen to advise a bipartisan group on AI safety, dubbing it “Humans First,” a term Allen had been using as a kind of rallying cry. The organization’s goal was to figure out how to galvanize regular people around AI, to demand that politicians in Washington put guardrails on a technology that threatens to potentially upend the existence and purpose of humanity. (No pressure.) The event that brought me to Georgia was the second leg of Humans First’s maiden voyage, fresh off a few stops in Florida.A motley audience filled about half a lecture hall at Georgia Tech that evening. Some were students, including members of a nascent AI safety club that had invited Allen. (Two told me they’d come only because of the posters put up around campus.) A camera guy from More Perfect Union, the leftist content channel that’s become a central hub for anti-data-center videos, hung around filming. Also in attendance was a well-heeled group of Atlantans in their thirties: two women with glossy, long hair and, seemingly, their partners.Up front, Jeremy Ornstein, a slight Humans First staffer with wild hair, started us off. Like a surprising number of Humans First staffers, Ornstein has a background in climate organizing. It showed: “A tiny group of people in control are racing ahead faster than ever with power and profit,” he warned, in a familiar, almost Obama-style cadence.Then Allen, sporting a belt with a big American flag buckle, strode up with a “Howdy, Georgia.” He stood before a whiteboard on which, earlier that day, he’d doodled a little Jetsons-style robot, a cheerful expression on its face as it aimed what looked like a ray gun at a group of stick figures with dazed expressions on their faces. “HUMANS FIRST,” Allen had written in big bubble letters, underlined four times.Allen’s critique of data centers verges on body horror.Photograph: Matt EichAllen played clips of Sam Altman intercut with footage of Marshall Applewhite, the leader of Heaven’s Gate. He told us, in his booming east Tennessee drawl, that Heaven’s Gate believers are a good metaphor for what AI leaders believe: Humanity must leave behind our physical bodies to ascend to the heavens, to meet the superintelligent beings living on the other side of the Hale-Bopp Comet. Everyone laughed a little nervously.Allen’s lectures follow a familiar pattern: jarringly right-wing talking points (at Georgia Tech, a Great Replacement joke!) smashed together with hallucinogenic nightmare descriptions of our future (the idea that a globalist cabal of tech oligarchs want to replace all of humanity with robots). A lot of it can sound completely insane, until you remember: Oh, right. Elon Musk does own a brain-chip implantation company. Sam Altman has blogged about how humans will “be the biological bootloader for digital intelligence and then fade into an evolutionary tree branch.”“Even if they were to create machines that were smarter than you, even if they created machines more powerful than you, you would have to continue to fight, because if you don't, you're a weakling,” Allen told the room. “If you don’t, you lay down and let the machine roll over you like a monster truck in a white-trash arena, and no one, no one wants that. No one but the most masochistic person wants that.” I found myself, surprisingly, suddenly, on the same page. Yeah! Hell yeah!Allen ended the speech with a cri de coeur: “To the greenies in the room, I say, Earth first! Right? Greenies?” (Not sure if that was directed at me.) “To the patriots in the room, I say, America first! And for anyone in the room with blood pulsing in their veins, anyone in the room with fire in their minds and hearts, you have to remember, in a machine age, humans first.” I nearly leaped to my feet.The “friends” Allen is now dragging me to meet turn out to be the well-dressed Atlantans I spotted at the talk, whom Allen had also just met. As he and I chase robots and drink whiskey before joining them, I ask if he has any nice memories of technology. He rattles off a couple typical alt-Gen-X-kid experiences: looking at Jane’s Addiction and Marilyn Manson’s websites; visiting a nascent Rotten.com. But the real shining moment in his relationship with the internet, Allen says, was discovering Ted Kaczynski.In his book, Allen vividly recalls coming across the Unabomber’s manifesto in the late 1990s while “surfing the web” at his community college writing lab. Kaczynski, a brilliant mathematician undone by the failings of the modern world, wrote “Industrial Society and Its Future” while mailing bombs to universities and business executives; The Washington Post and The New York Times were both encouraged to publish the manifesto as a way to make him stop. “Uncle Ted made more sense than any peacenik or techie cares to admit,” Allen writes.The influence is apparent. On War Room, Allen acts the part of a preacher at the pulpit warning us all of the coming dystopian age. A lot of his work is somewhat adjacent to body horror: What happens to our souls, he wonders, when our bodies and environments are increasingly digitized? I ask him why he thinks people hate data centers. He says: “If you ever see a fetus growing, and you see the brain growing and the neurons forming—it's amazing. Data centers, if you think about them as neurons of the Antichrist, that’s what we’re witnessing. The false messiah.”As we arrive at the restaurant, Allen’s new “friends” make space at their table and order some bread. One of them is Hannah Cox, a political influencer with more than 100,000 followers on X. Cox’s husband works in tech and, she tells me, has been “completely blackpilled” by the possibility of AI taking everyone’s jobs. Cox herself is “politically homeless” and came to Allen’s talk even though he’s not, she says, someone she’d usually listen to.Cox and I have very different social media feeds. When I follow up with her later, as the data center furor in Georgia reaches new heights, she tells me that everyone on her timeline seems to have agreed that data centers are being installed to conduct surveillance on the population. “It’s, I feel like, a ubiquitous fear,” she says. “Like it’s almost a bygone conclusion.”An Amazon Web Services data center in Ashburn, Virginia.Photograph: Getty ImagesTwo days after I drop Allen off at the airport, I drive out to Troup County, about an hour and a half south of Atlanta, to meet with a local activist named Gage Bailey. Although I arrive at the coffee shop 10 minutes early, Bailey is waiting for me. A stack of documents sits in front of him, color-coded in different highlighters, next to a massive iced drink with a bunch of whipped cream piled on top.Bailey, a Democrat with a degree in environmental science, first heard about data centers coming to town in the spring of 2025, when an acquaintance told him about one that might pop up on land that was formerly used by an industrial plastics developer. There were, he says, next to no public details about the project—how much power it was going to use, how much water it might draw from the local aquifer. He started doing research, compiling a 13-page memo extensively footnoted with primary sources, about the environmental impacts of data centers.Like many of the earliest folks involved in the movement, much of which has its origins in environmental concerns spread by groups like local Sierra Club chapters, Bailey began networking with fellow environmental advocates, learning to file public records requests by trial and error. Now, he manages a 4,000-person Facebook group and has helped with anti-data-center efforts in neighboring counties. His co-moderator is running for local office as a Democrat on an anti-data-center platform.There are a surprising number of Gage Baileys across Georgia, and more are rising up each day. National membership in data center opposition groups on Facebook has exploded in recent months, from under 100,000 in December to more than 500,000 by July. They’re not all Earth-hugging lefties. Shortly after I have coffee with Bailey, a woman in nearby Coweta County goes viral on right-wing media sounding the alarm that Georgia Power, the state’s deeply unpopular utility, is using various tactics to destroy her home and set up transmission lines for a data center—seemingly fulfilling Marjorie Taylor Greene’s Skynet prophecy.Bailey is hardly the type to watch War Room—he’s focused more on the slog of passing local ordinances than on Allen’s nightmarish visions of our robotic future. But as we talk, I wonder how Allen’s statements about tech oligarchs might land with him. Bailey learned last year that Google was the eventual tenant of the nearby data center project. He and some other environmental advocates had one meeting with Google in November, but afterward the tech giant ghosted them. Working with the company is “not going well,” he tells me. (In a statement to WIRED, Jamal Jessie, an Atlanta-based manager of community and workforce development at Google, said the company was focused on “direct, collaborative engagement with local schools, nonprofits, and civic organizations to deliver tangible regional benefits” and had formed a “$1 million partnership” with a local group helping people with their energy bills.) Bailey, who hasn’t been able to find a job in environmental science and works full-time at a convenience store, has a lot of ire for the world’s most powerful corporations trying to build AI in his backyard. “I don’t see a scenario, at least in the immediate future, in which we’re going to be able to trust these tech companies,” he says.Bailey’s Facebook group is still growing, and there’s been minimal political unrest so far, he says: Right or left, all members are opposed to data centers, and most of them are deeply skeptical of AI. These unlikely coalitions seem to be holding strong outside of Troup County, too. At a recent anti-data-center demonstration in New Jersey, I asked one mask-wearing protester—who told me they use “any” pronouns and are deeply concerned about the “ethics” of AI—about the right-wing influence on the movement. They shrugged uneasily. “Any enemy of my enemy is, at least, my temporary ally,” they said.After Atlanta, I can’t stop thinking about the Unabomber, so I brush up on his manifesto. I’d forgotten just how much Kaczynski blames “modern leftism”—with its advocacy for gay rights, feminism, and the like—for the “craziness of our world.” (To be fair, he was an equal-opportunity hater, writing that conservatives “are fools: They whine about the decay of traditional values, yet they enthusiastically support technological progress and economic growth.”) For Kaczynski, leftism was an inevitable byproduct of modern society, which pits humans against the natural order of the world and must be resisted.Kaczynski was, obviously, not someone to be emulated. But the idea that technology has a role in eroding our humanity is not an unpopular one. My girlfriend tells me a story about her high school English class: Her teacher handed out copies of two anonymized essays—one, a neatly organized dissertation about the pitfalls of technology; the other, a screed warning about the end of the world—and asked students to determine which was written by a sane person. The class overwhelmingly picked the essay about technology, and everyone agreed that the author had a great point. It was, of course, a trick question: Both were written by unreliable narrators, and the essay that resonated was an excerpt from “Industrial Society and Its Future.” Twenty years later, Luigi Mangione, who became an internet folk hero after allegedly shooting a UnitedHealthcare executive in late 2024, left a positive review of Kaczynski’s essay on GoodReads. Last year, PCMag—hardly a bastion of leftist anti-tech thinking—published an essay titled “The Unabomber Was Right.” As Allen writes in his book, Kaczynski also left a mark on some high-profile tech thinkers, including Ray Kurzweil, who wrote in 2000 that Kaczynski was “correct on the deeply entangled nature of the benefits and risks” of technology.Vent fans on the roof of a Digital Realty data center in Ashburn, Virginia.Photograph: Getty ImagesThere are echoes of Kaczynski, I think, in the resistance to renewable energy. In states like Vermont, it has turned crunchy hippie types against technology like solar and wind, and this resistance is now baked into some of the DNA of the anti-data-center movement. A 2025 study found that more than 450 counties and municipalities across nearly all states had some sort of solar or wind restrictions in place, a 16 percent increase from the year before. The Make America Healthy Again movement, too, can be viewed as an expression of a Kaczynski-esque environmentalism: the idea that modern society is poisoning our land, air, and water and that modern inventions like vaccines or antidepressants are actually bad for us. Many of these ideas can often collide in strange places. Currently, one of the top Substack writers in the site’s Climate and Environment category is a green-living farmer who has gone on the attack in recent months against solar installations in upstate New York, claiming (misleadingly) that the panels can poison the soil and destroy farmland.Allen’s book is a wilder read than “Industrial Society and Its Future.” The appendix, titled “My 55-Point Plan to Stay Human,” with suggestions like “Say hello to your neighbors” and “Buy a flip phone,” would be a hit at any leftist reading group in 2026 (perhaps with an edit to remove Allen’s insistence on “secure borders”). I agree with his assertion, moreover, that “it’s easy to imagine a day when … the specter of deadly AI is used to clamp down on freedom and erect miserable technocratic systems.” I do not, however, think the Covid-19 pandemic or “climate change” are examples of this already happening. Jennifer Bilek, a prominent anti-trans writer who claims that the medical-industrial complex has “infiltrated” gay and lesbian communities to push “transgenderism,” blurbed Allen’s book. When Allen recommends that I talk to her, I make an offhand remark that I don’t think she’d like me very much. “Oh, right,” he says, wiggling his eyebrows at me and referencing the pronouns listed on my X bio. “‘They/them.’”Right-wing anti-globalism isn’t the only way to do anti-AI populism, of course. The scholars Timnit Gebru and Émile Torres argue that the development of AI is mostly an excuse for the wealthy and powerful to exploit existing inequalities and push a eugenic agenda. (Gebru and Torres have also criticized AI safety groups, including the Center for AI Safety, which has given money to Humans First.) There’s also the religious way. In May, Pope Leo XIV released Magnifica Humanitas, his encyclical on AI, which advises humanity to develop technology responsibly and always be aware of the primacy of humanity. Like clockwork, a post popped up on my X feed of a photo of the Unabomber split with a photo of Leo. “You killed the man … But not the idea,” the caption read.Data centers, which are bringing together the most disparate neighbors in all regions of the country, may represent an opportunity to wage a real, unified fight against tech oligarchs. There’s a dream here, evident even in the pages of The New York Times, which in early May ran a headline that called data centers “the most bipartisan issue since beer.” The movement seems to envision a middle ground between rejecting technology wholesale—of truly Unabombering out—and rolling over and giving Big Tech everything it wants. But even if this middle ground does exist, it’s going to be a journey to reach it—one that our political system might not be prepared for.A Meta data center in Ashburn, Virginia.Photograph: Getty ImagesIn the weeks after I return from Georgia, it feels like the mainstream right fully takes over the data center conversation. People like Tucker Carlson and Matt Walsh make viral videos questioning the construction of specific projects. (By the way, Allen specifically wanted me to get this on the record: “Matt Walsh should have his beard plucked out like an Egyptian priest and be forced to kneel before Osiris. He copies my fucking shit all the time.” Walsh, through a spokesperson, disputes this.) Nancy Mace, running for governor in South Carolina, announces that she supports a yearlong moratorium. Florida governor Ron DeSantis, an outspoken AI and data center critic, signs first-of-its-kind legislation to ensure, in part, “that local governments maintain the authority to reject data center development in their communities.”Politics comes for Humans First too. In late March, there’s a high-profile spat online where pro-AI White House allies like Marc Andreessen and David Sacks retweet a piece critical of Humans First. Shortly after, the organization splits along partisan lines. The conservative wing keeps the Humans First name and makes the right-wing political activist Amy Kremer, who helped organize the January 6 “Save America” rally in DC, its chair; Allen leaves the group. When I ask Allen about the changeup, he is curiously coy (but characteristically body-horrible): The group was “undergoing mitosis,” he says. “I am now a lone organelle floating in the residual cytoplasm.”In mid-April, I go to DC for a Humans First event billed as the kickoff for the conservative arm. While I’m in town, I have this idea of taking Allen to visit an area of northern Virginia colloquially referred to as Data Center Alley, the densest stretch of data centers in the world, just about an hour outside the city. I reach out to a few operators to see if anyone will let us inside. It’s a weird email to send: I know everyone hates you right now, but could you let me into your facility to reassure everyone it’s not filled with poisonous water and haunted spirits? Almost immediately I receive polite nos. It’s for security reasons, one representative says.An AWS data center in Ashburn, Virginia.Photograph: Getty ImagesI end up driving around Data Center Alley anyway. (Allen is too busy to come.) I’m prepared to be a little underwhelmed—data centers are, as I’ve told countless people, just buildings. But I’m genuinely shocked by the sheer density of what’s here, how much construction I see, how impossibly big the buildings look edging up on the neatly manicured lawns of the wealthy northern Virginia suburbs. One of them, a Vantage facility partly painted a beautiful deep blue, is so loud that I can hear a constant, low-level hum even in the cul-de-sac across the street. I don’t know it yet, but months from now, Humans First will organize a national day of protest against data centers, with events in nearly 150 counties across 42 states.I park my car in the cul-de-sac and take out my notes from the night before, on a speech at the Humans First event given by a woman named Alicia Shamblin. Her 23-year-old son, Zane, killed himself last year after drinking hard ciders and talking to ChatGPT for hours; she and her husband are now suing OpenAI. Got his masters’ degree a few months earlier, my notes read. ChatGPT told him “Rest easy, king.” I wonder from which data center the LLM had sent that last message.Let us know what you think about this article. blocks.html_en: Data center resistance certainly has some of its roots in classic NIMBYism: Lots of Americans simply don’t trust stuff being built, in their backyards, by powerful companies for mysterious purposes. But the pace of the outrage that’s built up around the country is shocking. A recent Gallup poll showed that 70 percent of Americans would somewhat oppose or strongly oppose data center construction in their area. In the past few months, we’ve seen an attack on a pro-data-center council member (Indianapolis’ Ron Gibson); an attack on a tech CEO (OpenAI’s Sam Altman); data center moratoriums introduced in at least a dozen states (including Georgia) and passed in one (New York); and countless cities and counties passing their own bans or moratoriums, including in deep-red places like Hill County, Texas. People have been either arrested, detained, or escorted out while protesting data centers at public meetings in New Jersey, California, Wisconsin, and Indiana.

blocks.html_en: When I started reporting on data centers last year, Washington was, seemingly, completely unprepared for the backlash. blocks.html_en: Anger against data centers and public anxieties about AI are usually treated in polling and policy as separate topics: one an expression of environmental and civic worries, the other concerns about job loss and chatbots. But there's growing evidence that it's not so clear-cut. Research published in June of a small sample size of voters, for example, shows that very few people opposed to data centers actually live near them, and most of those who are against data centers are also skeptical of AI. Bannon, it seems, did a better job reading the room about how the American right might rebel against data centers, airing one segment last year that described data centers as “weapons labs” that are “being turned onto the population.”

blocks.html_en: Joe Allen has startlingly blue eyes behind professorial glasses and the shit-eating grin of the guy in high school who likes to tell non-PC jokes. He also has an origin story that’s catnip to lamestream media journalists like me. (And to less lamestream ones, apparently: When I ran into Allen at an event in New York, he was accompanied by Suzy Weiss from the Free Press, who informed me that she was also profiling Allen.) After touring internationally for years as a rigger for musical acts like the Black Eyed Peas and Calvin Harris, with a brief pause to get a master’s in theology from Boston University, Allen watched the music industry collapse during Covid. blocks.html_en: Allen arrived in this world as an outsider, able to speak its nerdy language with a mass-appeal, conspiracy-tinted flair. Since his book on transhumanism was published in 2023, Allen has interviewed AI critic Gary Marcus, debated futurist Max More and tech ethicist Nell Watson, and given a talk with a top official from the Golden Gate Institute for AI. The same day that Max Tegmark, an AI safety scholar and the leader of the Future of Life Institute, did an event with Bernie Sanders, he appeared on War Room with Allen and Bannon. The AI safety people began posting about Allen “in all their group chats,” one AI advocacy organization staffer told me. “Now everybody’s like, Joe! Joe! Joe!”

blocks.html_en: In late 2025, the Center for AI Safety recruited Allen to advise a bipartisan group on AI safety, dubbing it “Humans First,” a term Allen had been using as a kind of rallying cry. The organization’s goal was to figure out how to galvanize regular people around AI, to demand that politicians in Washington put guardrails on a technology that threatens to potentially upend the existence and purpose of humanity. (No pressure.) The event that brought me to Georgia was the second leg of Humans First’s maiden voyage, fresh off a few stops in Florida.

blocks.html_en: Allen’s lectures follow a familiar pattern: jarringly right-wing talking points (at Georgia Tech, a Great Replacement joke!) smashed together with hallucinogenic nightmare descriptions of our future (the idea that a globalist cabal of tech oligarchs want to replace all of humanity with robots). A lot of it can sound completely insane, until you remember: Oh, right. Elon Musk does own a brain-chip implantation company. Sam Altman has blogged about how humans will “be the biological bootloader for digital intelligence and then fade into an evolutionary tree branch.”

blocks.html_en: Kaczynski was, obviously, not someone to be emulated. But the idea that technology has a role in eroding our humanity is not an unpopular one. My girlfriend tells me a story about her high school English class: Her teacher handed out copies of two anonymized essays—one, a neatly organized dissertation about the pitfalls of technology; the other, a screed warning about the end of the world—and asked students to determine which was written by a sane person. The class overwhelmingly picked the essay about technology, and everyone agreed that the author had a great point. It was, of course, a trick question: Both were written by unreliable narrators, and the essay that resonated was an excerpt from “Industrial Society and Its Future.” Twenty years later, Luigi Mangione, who became an internet folk hero after allegedly shooting a UnitedHealthcare executive in late 2024, left a positive review of Kaczynski’s essay on GoodReads. Last year, PCMag—hardly a bastion of leftist anti-tech thinking—published an essay titled “The Unabomber Was Right.” As Allen writes in his book, Kaczynski also left a mark on some high-profile tech thinkers, including Ray Kurzweil, who wrote in 2000 that Kaczynski was “correct on the deeply entangled nature of the benefits and risks” of technology.

blocks.html_en: There are echoes of Kaczynski, I think, in the resistance to renewable energy. In states like Vermont, it has turned crunchy hippie types against technology like solar and wind, and this resistance is now baked into some of the DNA of the anti-data-center movement. A 2025 study found that more than 450 counties and municipalities across nearly all states had some sort of solar or wind restrictions in place, a 16 percent increase from the year before. The Make America Healthy Again movement, too, can be viewed as an expression of a Kaczynski-esque environmentalism: the idea that modern society is poisoning our land, air, and water and that modern inventions like vaccines or antidepressants are actually bad for us. Many of these ideas can often collide in strange places. Currently, one of the top Substack writers in the site’s Climate and Environment category is a green-living farmer who has gone on the attack in recent months against solar installations in upstate New York, claiming (misleadingly) that the panels can poison the soil and destroy farmland.

blocks.html_en: Data centers, which are bringing together the most disparate neighbors in all regions of the country, may represent an opportunity to wage a real, unified fight against tech oligarchs. There’s a dream here, evident even in the pages of The New York Times, which in early May ran a headline that called data centers “the most bipartisan issue since beer.” The movement seems to envision a middle ground between rejecting technology wholesale—of truly Unabombering out—and rolling over and giving Big Tech everything it wants. content_html_zh:
乔·艾伦想知道这个机器人的名字是什么。 起初，我认为我们在酒店酒吧喝下的双倍威士忌一定是让他着迷了，因为他像一个课间休息的孩子一样冲向送货车。 我对时间感到焦虑：我应该开车送艾伦去机场，万福玛丽努力让他在离开亚特兰大之前单独进行一次适当的谈话。

几周来，我一直在与艾伦来回交流，他在史蒂夫·班农 (Steve Bannon) 的战争室播客中以反科技预言家的身份而闻名全国，寻求加入日益激烈的反对人工智能运动。 我来到数据中心抵制的热点佐治亚州，听艾伦的一场演讲，他一直在全国各地进行演讲。 但当我到达活动现场时，他告诉我他必须立即离开。

幸运的是，他的航班不断推迟，这意味着我可以跟随他完成各种支线任务——比如这个，去附近的一家餐馆见一些朋友。 他设法回避了我关于他们身份的大部分问题，将话题转向更有趣的事情，比如“逆奇点”（他认为，随着我们越来越依赖人工智能获取信息，人类将接近我们的智力和创造力崩溃的地步）。 艾伦在餐厅的朋友们似乎也对我知之甚少。 在我们途中，其中一人打电话给艾伦询问预计到达时间。 “我带来了一个朋友——嗯，一个亦敌亦友的人，”他说，戏剧性地斜视了我一眼。

亚特兰大市中心到处都有送货机器人，这是少数几个主要大都市区之一，它们正在为人们送汉堡或炸玉米饼。 艾伦追上了这个——我惊讶地发现它的前面有眼睛形状的发光白光——并在旁边读到了一个名字：“CJ”。 我想起了艾伦最近的书《黑暗永恒：超人类主义和反人类战争》的书名，我想知道这个机器人取代的送货员发生了什么事。 它的眼睛可怜兮兮、无力地看着我。

当人们问我在佐治亚州做什么时，我会告诉他们一些简单的事情。 我说，人们讨厌数据中心，所以我想弄清楚他们是否也讨厌人工智能。 这都是真的。 但这个话题也让我很烦恼。 在我多年来有关能源和环境的报道中，我从未见过像对数据中心那样的尖酸刻薄，也从未见过围绕数据中心的建设而产生的近乎宗教的愤怒，也从未见过这种抵制似乎将来自政治光谱完全相反两端的人们团结起来的方式。

当我写这篇文章时，一位朋友从 X 上的“白人基督教民族主义”帐户向我发送了一条帖子：一幅看似由人工智能生成的卡通画，烟熏熊站在一个燃烧的类似数据中心的结构前，上面写着“只有你才能阻止数据中心”。 怎么了？ 我的朋友问。 我会尝试解释一下。

曾几何时，您可能一直住在数据中心旁边，但从未听说过它。

在过去的几十年里，数据中心在美国各地悄然建立，主要是在既有光纤连接又靠近电力的地区——硅谷和华盛顿地区是受欢迎的选择。 他们帮助播放 Netflix 或在云中存储内容，或者做我们经常在网上做的无数愚蠢而重要的事情中的任何一件。

然后是 ChatGPT 和 AI 竞赛。 科技寡头们突然提出，我们需要尽快建立尽可能多的数据中心。 他们在演讲、新闻采访和社交媒体帖子中表示，打造最好的人工智能需要大规模的建设，尤其是超大规模的建设——我们已经拥有的结构的庞然大物版本。 特朗普政府对此表示认同，取消了环境法规，让政府不再阻碍发展。

随着公司急于寻找最便宜的土地、电力和水，数据中心开始随处可见。 每天都会有更引人注目的头条新闻。 据报道，埃隆·马斯克用卡车将未经许可的燃气轮机运往他的孟菲斯 xAI 园区，该园区位于一个以黑人为主的社区，已经遭受了严重的污染和污染。 《华盛顿邮报》一篇颇受欢迎（后来引起争议）的文章估计，一次 ChatGPT 搜索消耗的电量相当于一瓶水。 人们关注他们的电费，因为新的数据中心负载导致公用事业公司预测需求将极高。 如果你相信各种经济渠道，那么数据中心建设现在几乎支撑着整个美国经济。 所有这一切都发生在科技首席执行官们公开思考人工智能将如何抢走每个人的工作并取代人类创造力本身的时候。

人们自然而然地开始提问。

数据中心的抵制肯定有一些根源于经典的邻避主义：许多美国人根本不相信强大的公司在他们的后院出于神秘目的而建造的东西。 但全国各地愤怒情绪的蔓延速度令人震惊。 最近的盖洛普民意调查显示，70% 的美国人会有些反对或强烈反对在他们所在地区建设数据中心。 在过去的几个月里，我们看到了针对支持数据中心的理事会成员（印第安纳波利斯的罗恩·吉布森）的攻击；对科技首席执行官（OpenAI 的 Sam Altman）的攻击；至少有十几个州（包括乔治亚州）暂停了数据中心，并在一个州（纽约州）获得通过；无数城市和县也通过了自己的禁令或暂停令，包括德克萨斯州希尔县等深红色地区。 在新泽西州、加利福尼亚州、威斯康星州和印第安纳州举行的公开集会上抗议数据中心时，人们要么被逮捕、拘留，要么被护送出境。

当我去年开始报道数据中心时，华盛顿似乎对这种强烈反对完全没有做好准备。 它对任何与人工智能相关的事情都没有做好准备，对于国会里挤满了几乎无法使用手机的人来说，这真的不足为奇。 我看到的最早呼吁数据中心发展的两位国家政治家是右翼民粹主义者 Marjorie Taylor Greene 和 Thomas Massie，他们担心如何利用拟议的 10 年国家级人工智能法规禁令在私有财产上建设数据中心。 格林在 2025 年 6 月发推文称：“强迫人们的私人财产征用以连接未来的天网，这并不是很共和党的做法。”

与此同时，特朗普的前顾问、长期的技术批评者史蒂夫·班农 (Steve Bannon) 在艾伦的指导下定期在作战室讨论人工智能问题。 2025 年底，当特朗普政府试图重新实施监管禁令时，班农领导的 MAGA 联盟出面阻止了这一举措。 班农去年秋天告诉美国广播公司新闻，艾伦是他计划的关键部分：“他会参加所有可能的会议，会见人们...... 我告诉他，我希望你去每一个需要你的教堂。 我想让你去参加 MAGA、茶党会议。 我想在底层了解这一点。”

对数据中心的愤怒和公众对人工智能的焦虑通常在民意调查和政策中被视为不同的主题：一个是对环境和公民担忧的表达，另一个是对失业和聊天机器人的担忧。 但越来越多的证据表明，情况并不那么明确。 例如，6月份发布的针对小样本选民的研究表明，反对数据中心的人实际上很少住在数据中心附近，而且大多数反对数据中心的人也对人工智能持怀疑态度。 班农似乎在解读美国右翼可能如何反抗数据中心方面做得更好，他在去年播出的一段节目中将数据中心描述为“武器实验室”，“正在向民众提供服务”。

我无法摆脱这样的感觉：民粹主义右翼知道一些我不知道的事情——关于人工智能，关于美国人对科技和建筑环境的态度。 甚至关于我们可能会带着这一切去往何处。 这就是为什么在一月份，我第一次联系艾伦。

乔·艾伦（Joe Allen）在教授眼镜后面有一双惊人的蓝眼睛，脸上挂着高中生喜欢讲非电脑笑话的令人吃屎的笑容。 他还有一个起源故事，对像我这样的蹩脚媒体记者来说很有吸引力。 （显然，对于不那么蹩脚的人来说：当我在纽约的一次活动中遇到艾伦时，他是由《自由报》的苏西·韦斯陪同的，她告诉我她也在对艾伦进行侧写。） 艾伦在黑眼豆豆乐队和卡尔文·哈里斯等音乐团体中担任了多年的国际巡演员，并短暂停顿并获得了波士顿大学的神学硕士学位，之后艾伦目睹了音乐产业在新冠疫情期间崩溃。 他一直在为极右和极左媒体撰写有关技术之恶的文章，这是他长期以来的兴趣所在。2021 年，当史蒂夫·班农 (Steve Bannon) 的制片人打电话邀请他参加《作战室》时，他住在一辆面包车里；不久之后，班农向他提供了一份科技记者的工作。 艾伦曾一度住在华盛顿的一套公寓里，War Room 就是在那里录制的。

人工智能安全和道德的世界是乱伦的，正常人几乎完全无法进入，而且充满了主要居住在伦敦或湾区的人。 （事实上​​，许多备受瞩目的人工智能安全研究人员的总部都位于伯克利的一个办公大楼。） 他们都在争论我们是否会被无所不知的超级智能消灭，因此应该放慢或停止人工智能的发展，或者同样的超级智能是否会带领我们走向涅槃，因此应该尽快发展。

艾伦以一个局外人的身份来到这个世界，能够以一种具有大众吸引力、带有阴谋色彩的天赋说出这个世界的书呆子语言。 自 2023 年出版有关超人类主义的书以来，艾伦采访了人工智能评论家加里·马库斯 (Gary Marcus)，与未来学家马克斯·莫尔 (Max More) 和技术伦理学家内尔·沃森 (Nell Watson) 进行了辩论，并与金门人工智能研究所的一位高级官员进行了交谈。 人工智能安全学者、未来生命研究所负责人马克斯·泰格马克 (Max Tegmark) 与伯尼·桑德斯 (Bernie Sanders) 一起举办活动的同一天，他与艾伦和班农一起出现在作战室。 一位人工智能倡导组织的工作人员告诉我，人工智能安全人员开始在“所有群聊中”发布有关艾伦的信息。 “现在每个人都说，乔！ 乔！ 乔！”

2025 年末，人工智能安全中心招募艾伦为一个两党团体提供有关人工智能安全的建议，并将其称为“人类第一”，艾伦一直用这个词作为一种战斗口号。 该组织的目标是找出如何激励普通人关注人工智能，要求华盛顿的政治家对可能颠覆人类存在和目的的技术设置护栏。 （没有压力。） 把我带到佐治亚州的活动是人类第一号首航的第二站，刚刚在佛罗里达州停留了几站。

那天晚上，佐治亚理工学院的演讲厅里挤满了形形色色的观众。 其中一些是学生，其中包括邀请艾伦的新兴人工智能安全俱乐部的成员。 （有两个人告诉我，他们来这里只是因为校园周围张贴的海报。） More Perfect Union 是一个左翼内容频道，现已成为反数据中心视频的中心枢纽，一名摄影师在现场进行拍摄。 出席的还有一群三十多岁的富有的亚特兰大人：两名有着光滑长发的女性，似乎还有她们的伴侣。

在前面，杰里米·奥恩斯坦（Jeremy Ornstein）为我们引路，他是人类第一组织的一名身材瘦小、头发蓬乱的员工。 与数量惊人的“人类第一”组织的员工一样，奥恩斯坦也有气候组织方面的背景。 它表明：“一小群掌握权力的人正在以比以往任何时候都更快的速度与权力和利润赛跑，”他用一种熟悉的、几乎是奥巴马风格的语调警告说。

然后，艾伦系着一条带有大美国国旗扣的腰带，大步走来，喊着“你好，佐治亚州”。 那天早些时候，他站在一块白板上，在上面涂鸦了一个《杰森一家》风格的小机器人，当它用看起来像射线枪的东西瞄准一群表情茫然的简笔画时，它脸上露出欢快的表情。 “人类第一，”艾伦用大气泡字母写道，并划了四次下划线。

艾伦播放了山姆·奥尔特曼的片段和天堂之门领袖马歇尔·阿普尔怀特的片段。 他用田纳西州东部的慢吞吞的声音告诉我们，“天堂之门”的信徒很好地比喻了人工智能领袖的信念：人类必须离开我们的身体才能升入天堂，去见生活在海尔-波普彗星另一边的超级智能生物。 大家都笑得有些紧张。

艾伦的讲座遵循一个熟悉的模式：刺耳的右翼谈话要点（在佐治亚理工学院，一个伟大的替代笑话！） 与对我们未来的令人产生幻觉的噩梦描述（科技寡头的全球主义阴谋集团想要用机器人取代全人类的想法）粉碎在一起。 其中很多听起来完全疯狂，直到你记住：哦，对了。 埃隆·马斯克确实拥有一家脑芯片植入公司。 萨姆·奥尔特曼 (Sam Altman) 在博客中谈到了人类将如何“成为数字智能的生物引导程序，然后逐渐融入进化树枝。”

“即使他们创造了比你更聪明的机器，即使他们创造了比你更强大的机器，你也必须继续战斗，因为如果你不这样做，你就是一个弱者，”艾伦告诉房间。 “如果你不这样做，你就会躺下来，让机器从你身上碾过，就像一辆巨型卡车在白色垃圾场上碾压一样，没有人、没有人愿意这样。 除了最受虐狂的人之外，没有人想要这样。” 令人惊讶的是，我突然发现自己站在了同一立场上。 是的！ 是啊！

艾伦以一声大喊结束了演讲：“我对房间里的绿色环保人士说，地球第一！ 正确的？ 绿党？” （不确定这是不是针对我的。） “我对在座的爱国者们说，美国优先！ 对于房间里的每个人，血管里的血液在跳动，房间里的每个人的思想和内心都充满火焰，你必须记住，在机器时代，人类优先。” 我几乎跳了起来。

艾伦现在拖着我去见的“朋友”原来是我在演讲中看到的穿着考究的亚特兰大人，艾伦也刚刚认识了他们。 当我和他追逐机器人并在加入它们之前喝威士忌时，我问他对科技是否有任何美好的回忆。 他滔滔不绝地讲述了一些典型的另类 X 世代孩子的经历：浏览 Jane’s Addiction 和 Marilyn Manson 的网站；访问新生的 Rotten.com。 但艾伦说，他与互联网关系中真正的闪光时刻是发现了特德·卡钦斯基。

艾伦在书中生动地回忆了 20 世纪 90 年代末在他的社区大学写作实验室“上网”时看到大学炸弹客宣言的情景。 卡钦斯基是一位因现代世界的失败而崩溃的杰出数学家，他在向大学和企业高管邮寄炸弹的同时写下了《工业社会及其未来》； 《华盛顿邮报》和《纽约时报》都被鼓励发表这份宣言，以此来阻止他。 “泰德叔叔的说法比任何和平主义者或技术人员都愿意承认的更有意义，”艾伦写道。

影响力是显而易见的。 在《战争室》中，艾伦在讲坛上扮演传教士的角色，警告我们所有人即将到来的反乌托邦时代。 他的很多作品都与身体恐怖有些相似：他想知道，当我们的身体和环境日益数字化时，我们的灵魂会发生什么？ 我问他为什么认为人们讨厌数据中心。 他说：“如果你看到胎儿在生长，你看到大脑在生长，神经元在形成，那真是太神奇了。 数据中心，如果你将它们视为敌基督的神经元，那就是我们所目睹的。 假弥赛亚。”

当我们到达餐厅时，艾伦的新“朋友”在他们的餐桌上腾出空间并点了一些面包。 其中之一是汉娜·考克斯 (Hannah Cox)，她是一位在 X 上拥有超过 10 万粉丝的政治影响者。 考克斯的丈夫在科技行业工作，她告诉我，人工智能可能会取代所有人的工作，让他“彻底蒙羞”。 考克斯本人是“政治上的无家可归者”，尽管她说艾伦不是她通常会听的人，但她还是来听艾伦的演讲。

考克斯和我的社交媒体内容截然不同。 当我稍后跟进她时，随着佐治亚州数据中心的愤怒达到新的高度，她告诉我，她时间线上的每个人似乎都同意正在安装数据中心来对人口进行监视。 “我觉得这是一种无处不在的恐惧，”她说。 “就像这几乎是一个既定的结论一样。”

我把艾伦送到机场两天后，我开车前往亚特兰大以南约一个半小时车程的特鲁普县，会见当地一位名叫盖奇·贝利 (Gage Bailey) 的活动人士。 虽然我提前10分钟到达咖啡店，Bailey已经在等我了。 他面前放着一叠文件，用不同的荧光笔进行颜色编码，旁边是一大杯冰饮料，上面堆着一堆生奶油。

拥有环境科学学位的民主党人贝利第一次听说数据中心将在 2025 年春天落户该镇，当时一位熟人告诉他，一个数据中心可能会出现在以前由工业塑料开发商使用的土地上。 他说，几乎没有关于该项目的公开细节——它将使用多少电力，可能从当地含水层抽取多少水。 他开始进行研究，编写了一份长达 13 页的备忘录，并附有大量关于数据中心对环境影响的主要来源的脚注。

与许多最早参与该运动的人一样，贝利开始与其他环保倡导者建立联系，通过反复试验学习提交公共记录请求，其中大部分源于当地塞拉俱乐部分会等团体传播的环境问题。 现在，他管理着一个 4,000 人的 Facebook 群组，并帮助邻近县的反数据中心工作。 他的联合主持人正在以反数据中心的平台作为民主党人竞选当地办公室。

佐治亚州各地的盖奇贝利 (Gage Bailey) 数量惊人，而且每天都有更多的人在崛起。 近几个月来，Facebook 上数据中心反对团体的全国会员人数激增，从 12 月的不到 10 万增加到 7 月的超过 50 万。 他们并不都是热爱地球的左撇子。 我和贝利喝完咖啡后不久，附近考韦塔县的一名妇女在右翼媒体上疯传，她发出警报称，该州极不受欢迎的公用事业公司佐治亚电力正在使用各种策略摧毁她的房屋并为数据中心建立传输线路，这似乎正在实现马乔里·泰勒·格林的天网预言。

贝利并不是那种会看《作战室》的人——他更关注的是通过当地法令的艰辛，而不是艾伦对我们机器人未来的噩梦般的愿景。 但在我们交谈时，我想知道艾伦关于科技寡头的言论会如何影响他。 贝利去年了解到，谷歌是附近数据中心项目的最终租户。 去年 11 月，他和其他一些环保倡导者与谷歌进行了一次会面，但后来这家科技巨头却避开了他们。 他告诉我，与公司的合作“并不顺利”。 （谷歌驻亚特兰大的社区和劳动力发展经理贾马尔·杰西（Jamal Jessie）在给《连线》杂志的一份声明中表示，该公司专注于“与当地学校、非营利组织和民间组织直接合作，以提供切实的地区利益”，并与当地一家帮助人们解决能源账单的组织建立了“100万美元的合作伙伴关系”。） 贝利一直未能找到环境科学方面的工作，只能在一家便利店全职工作，他对世界上最强大的公司试图在他的后院构建人工智能感到非常愤怒。 “我认为，至少在不久的将来，我们无法信任这些科技公司，”他说。

贝利的 Facebook 群组仍在不断壮大，到目前为止，政治动荡微乎其微，他说：无论是左派还是右派，所有成员都反对数据中心，其中大多数人对人工智能深表怀疑。 这些不太可能的联盟似乎在特鲁普县以外也保持着强大的力量。 最近在新泽西州举行的一次反数据中心示威活动中，我向一位戴口罩的抗议者询问了右翼对该运动的影响，他告诉我他们使用“任何”代词，并且对人工智能的“道德”深感担忧。 他们不安地耸耸肩。 “我敌人的任何敌人至少都是我暂时的盟友，”他们说。

亚特兰大之后，我无法停止思考大学炸弹客，所以我温习了他的宣言。 我忘记了卡钦斯基是如何将“我们世界的疯狂”归咎于“现代左派”——倡导同性恋权利、女权主义等。 （公平地说，他是一个机会均等的仇恨者，他写道，保守派“都是傻瓜：他们抱怨传统价值观的衰落，但他们却热情支持技术进步和经济增长。”）对于卡钦斯基来说，左派主义是现代社会不可避免的副产品，它使人类与世界的自然秩序对立，必须受到抵制。

显然，卡钦斯基不是一个值得效仿的人。 但技术会侵蚀我们人性的想法并不是一个不受欢迎的想法。 我的女朋友给我讲了一个关于她高中英语课的故事：她的老师分发了两篇匿名论文的副本——一篇是关于技术陷阱的组织整齐的论文；另一篇是一篇关于技术陷阱的论文。另一篇是一篇关于世界末日的长篇文章，并要求学生们判断哪一篇是由一个理智的人写的。 全班同学压倒性地选择了这篇关于技术的文章，每个人都认为作者的观点很好。 当然，这是一个棘手的问题：这两篇文章都是由不可靠的叙述者写的，引起共鸣的文章是《工业社会及其未来》的摘录。 二十年后，路易吉·曼吉奥内 (Luigi Mangione) 在 GoodReads 上对卡钦斯基的文章留下了正面评价。据称，他在 2024 年底枪杀了联合医疗保健公司 (UnitedHealthcare) 的一名高管，成为互联网民间英雄。 去年，PCMag——算不上是左派反科技思想的堡垒——发表了一篇题为《大学炸弹客是对的》的文章。 正如艾伦在书中所写，卡辛斯基也给一些知名科技思想家留下了印记，其中包括雷·库兹韦尔 (Ray Kurzweil)，他在 2000 年写道，卡辛斯基“对技术的利益和风险的深刻纠缠本质的看法是正确的”。

我认为，在抵制可再生能源方面，有卡钦斯基的影子。 在佛蒙特州等州，顽皮的嬉皮士开始反对太阳能和风能等技术，这种抵制现在已经融入了反数据中心运动的某些基因中。 2025 年的一项研究发现，几乎所有州的 450 多个县和市都实施了某种太阳能或风能限制，比前一年增加了 16%。 “让美国再次健康”运动也可以被视为卡钦斯基式环保主义的表达：现代社会正在毒害我们的土地、空气和水，而疫苗或抗抑郁药等现代发明实际上对我们有害。 其中许多想法经常会在奇怪的地方发生冲突。 目前，该网站“气候与环境”类别中的顶级 Substack 作者之一是一位绿色生活农民，近几个月来，他一直在攻击纽约州北部的太阳能装置，声称（误导性地）太阳能电池板会毒害土壤并破坏农田。

艾伦的书比《工业社会及其未来》更值得一读。 该附录的标题是“我保持人性的 55 点计划”，其中包括“向邻居问好”和“买一部翻盖手机”等建议，到 2026 年，它将在任何左翼阅读团体中引起轰动（也许需要进行编辑以删除艾伦对“安全边界”的坚持）。 此外，我同意他的说法，“很容易想象有一天...... 致命人工智能的幽灵被用来压制自由并建立悲惨的技术官僚体系。” 然而，我并不认为 Covid-19 大流行或“气候变化”是这种情况已经发生的例子。 著名反跨性别作家詹妮弗·比莱克 (Jennifer Bilek) 声称，医疗工业综合体已经“渗透”同性恋社区，以推动“跨性别主义”，她对艾伦的书做了模糊的描述。 当艾伦建议我和她谈谈时，我随口说我认为她不太喜欢我。 “哦，对了，”他一边说，一边对我摇动眉毛，并引用了我 X 简历上列出的代词。 “‘他们/他们。’”

当然，右翼反全球主义并不是反人工智能民粹主义的唯一途径。 学者蒂姆尼特·格布鲁（Timnit Gebru）和埃米尔·托雷斯（Émile Torres）认为，人工智能的发展主要是富人和有权势的人利用现有不平等现象和推动优生议程的借口。 （格布鲁和托雷斯还批评了人工智能安全组织，包括向人类优先组织捐款的人工智能安全中心。） 还有宗教的方式。 今年五月，教皇利奥十四世发布了他关于人工智能的通谕《Magnifica Humanitas》，建议人类负责任地开发技术，并始终意识到人类的首要地位。 就像发条一样，我的 X feed 上弹出了一张帖子，其中有一张大学炸弹客的照片和一张 Leo 的照片。 “你杀了那个人…… 但不是这个想法，”标题写道。

数据中心将全国各地区最不同的邻居聚集在一起，这可能代表着一个机会，可以与科技寡头进行真正的、统一的斗争。 这里有一个梦想，甚至在《纽约时报》的版面中也很明显，该报 5 月初的标题称数据中心是“自啤酒以来最两党合作的问题”。 该运动似乎设想了一个中间立场，即拒绝技术批发（真正的“Unabombering”）和翻转并给予大型科技公司想要的一切。 但即使这个中间立场确实存在，实现它也将是一个漫长的过程——我们的政治体系可能还没有做好准备。

在我从佐治亚州回来后的几周内，感觉主流右翼完全接管了数据中心的话题。 塔克·卡尔森和马特·沃尔什等人制作了病毒视频，质疑特定项目的建设。 （顺便说一句，艾伦特别希望我将这一点记录在案：“马特·沃尔什应该像埃及牧师一样拔掉胡子，并被迫跪在奥西里斯面前。 他他妈的总是抄袭我的狗屎。” 沃尔什通过发言人对此提出异议。） 竞选南卡罗来纳州州长的南希·梅斯宣布她支持为期一年的暂停。 佛罗里达州州长罗恩·德桑蒂斯（Ron DeSantis）是一位直言不讳的人工智能和数据中心批评者，他签署了首个此类立法，以在一定程度上确保“地方政府保留拒绝在其社区开发数据中心的权力”。

政治也是以人为本。 3 月下旬，网上发生了一场备受瞩目的争吵，马克·安德森 (Marc Andreessen) 和大卫·萨克斯 (David Sacks) 等支持人工智能的白宫盟友转发了一篇批评“人类优先”的文章。 不久之后，该组织因党派分歧而分裂。 保守派保留了“人类第一”的名字，并任命右翼政治活动家艾米·克莱默(Amy Kremer)为主席，艾米·克莱默曾帮助组织了1月6日在华盛顿举行的“拯救美国”集会。艾伦离开了队伍。 当我向艾伦询问这一变化时，他奇怪地腼腆（但典型的身体可怕）：他说，这个群体“正在经历有丝分裂”。 “我现在是一个孤独的细胞器，漂浮在残留的细胞质中。”

四月中旬，我去华盛顿参加一场“人类第一”活动，该活动被宣传为保守派的开局。 当我在城里时，我有一个想法，带艾伦去参观弗吉尼亚州北部的一个地区，俗称数据中心巷，这是世界上数据中心最密集的区域，距离城市仅一小时车程。 我联系了几位接线员，看看是否有人会让我们进去。 这是一封奇怪的电子邮件：我知道现在每个人都讨厌你，但是你能让我进入你的设施，让每个人放心，那里没有充满毒水和闹鬼的灵魂吗？ 我几乎立刻就收到了礼貌的拒绝。 一位代表表示，这是出于安全原因。

不管怎样，我最终还是开车绕着数据中心巷转。 （艾伦太忙了，没来。） 我准备好有点不知所措了——正如我告诉无数人的那样，数据中心只是建筑物。 但我真的对这里的密度感到震惊，我看到了如此之多的建筑，这些建筑在弗吉尼亚州北部富裕郊区修剪整齐的草坪上看起来有多么巨大。 其中一个是 Vantage 设施，部分漆成美丽的深蓝色，声音非常大，即使在街对面的死胡同里，我也能听到持续不断的低声嗡嗡声。 我还不知道，但几个月后，Humans First 将组织全国反对数据中心的抗议活动，活动将在 42 个州的近 150 个县举行。

我把车停在死胡同里，拿出前一天晚上的笔记，内容是一位名叫艾丽西亚·尚布林 (Alicia Shamblin) 的女士在“人类第一”活动上发表的演讲。 她 23 岁的儿子 Zane 去年在喝烈性苹果酒并与 ChatGPT 聊了几个小时后自杀了；她和她的丈夫现在正在起诉 OpenAI。 我的笔记上写着，几个月前他获得了硕士学位。 ChatGPT 告诉他“放心吧，国王。” 我想知道法学硕士从哪个数据中心发送了最后一条消息。
